name: Vieux-Quebec
tagline: Walled stone streets and the only fortified old town in North America
description: Inside the stone walls, Vieux-Quebec is cobbled streets, seventeenth and eighteenth century houses and the Chateau Frontenac above the river. Upper Town holds the ramparts and Dufferin Terrace, Lower Town holds Petit-Champlain and Place Royale. It is beautiful, compact and entirely walkable, but it belongs to visitors more than residents.
bestFor: Short stay nomads who want to wake up inside a UNESCO old town.
pros: Completely walkable, no car needed at all
Endless cafes and terraces within the walls
Ramparts and riverside promenade on your doorstep
cons: Tourist crowds and prices from June to October
Steep hills and stairs everywhere, hard in winter ice
Very few long term rentals, mostly short stay units

name: Saint-Roch
tagline: The old industrial low town rebuilt as the tech and cafe quarter
description: Down the cliff from the old town, Saint-Roch runs along Rue Saint-Joseph with roasters, microbreweries, galleries and the largest cluster of tech offices and co-working space in the city. Converted brick buildings and new condos house a young working crowd, and it stays flat and easy to walk.
bestFor: Remote workers who want co-working, coffee and flat walkable streets.
pros: Best co-working and specialty coffee density in the city
Flat terrain, unlike the hilly old town
cons: Some blocks feel rough and empty after dark
Highway overpasses cut the district in places
Winter wind funnels through the wide streets

name: Saint-Jean-Baptiste
tagline: Colourful walk-ups on a hill just outside the walls
description: Squeezed between the walls and Saint-Roch, this is the most residential of the central districts, brightly painted three storey walk-ups with exterior staircases along Rue Saint-Jean. Independent bistros, record shops and neighbourhood bars fill the strip, and the crowd is local rather than touristic.
bestFor: Nomads who want central living with locals instead of tour groups.
pros: Walkable to both the old town and Saint-Roch
Cheaper apartments than inside the walls
Excellent small bistros and bars along Rue Saint-Jean
cons: Steep hill, and the escalier to Saint-Roch is icy in winter
Older buildings with thin walls and noisy neighbours

name: Montcalm
tagline: The arts district on the Grande Allee with mature trees
description: West of the walls along Grande Allee and Avenue Cartier, Montcalm is stone and brick homes on wide tree lined streets, with the Musee national des beaux-arts, theatres and the Plains of Abraham next door. Avenue Cartier is a compact strip of food shops, bakeries and cafes. It is calm and clearly upper middle class.
bestFor: Nomads on longer stays who want quiet streets and a big park for running.
pros: Plains of Abraham for running, skiing and cycling
Avenue Cartier food shops and cafes on foot
Quiet, safe residential streets at night
cons: Rents run above the city average
Grande Allee bar strip gets loud on summer weekends
A 20 minute walk or bus ride to Saint-Roch coworking

name: Limoilou
tagline: A grid of triplexes across the river with the lowest rents
description: Across the Saint-Charles river from Saint-Roch, Limoilou is a flat numbered street grid of brick triplexes with the 3e Avenue commercial strip running through it. Families, students and artists live here, and the neighbourhood has quietly grown cafes, breweries and bakeries while keeping the cheapest central rents.
bestFor: Budget nomads and anyone staying a full season who wants space for the money.
pros: Cheapest rents of the central districts
Flat grid, very good for cycling and walking
Growing cafe, bakery and brewery strip on 3e Avenue
cons: A 25 to 30 minute walk or a bus to the old town
Highway and rail noise on the western edges
Fewer services once you leave the 3e Avenue strip
